title: The Skeptic's Benchmark
youtubeTitle: Does Tensorized Verilog Actually Help? An Honest HELUT Benchmark
description: A technically informed skeptic asks the right questions: what problem does tensorizing a synthesized circuit solve, is it more efficient than native HDL execution, and why target Apple silicon? This episode answers with a sealed matched-circuit receipt rather than a selected timing. On one 8-bit ripple adder, the historical warmed-graph comparison shows graph amortization against scalar Verilator, but the accepted paired scope counts deterministic preparation, synchronized execution, strict readback, and the same ordered digest on both sides. At B=65,536 HELUT measured 8.544 milliseconds versus 7.422 milliseconds for 16-worker Verilator: HELUT remained 15.1 percent slower, with no paired crossover through that width. The digest is required shared work inside both timers and is not subtracted to synthesize a separate evaluator ratio. A separate HELUT graph sweep reaches 1,048,576 lanes, but high-width native values are projections on another fixture, not same-width paired results. The episode also preserves the lane-distinct correctness gate: 65,536 distinct assignments, 589,824 checked output bits, zero mismatches, and a corruption control that moves the digest. A 688-LUT, 26-DFF Enigma M3 netlist separately runs through HELUT's trivial, noise-free N=1024 Metal path and agrees with the clear oracle on a 25-letter transcript. Apple silicon matters here because host orchestration, Metal shaders, and MPSGraph share one physical memory pool; that is an architectural rationale, not a measured win over a discrete GPU. No encryption, sequential-lane throughput, general HDL superiority, CXXRTL result, Apple exclusivity, or cross-platform conclusion is claimed. Epoch C71.

scenes.headline: Does tensorized Verilog actually help?
scenes.subhead: The method behind the number, not the pitch.
scenes.voiceover: Episode zero answers what HELUT is and where it loses. This episode is the receipt underneath that answer: how the comparison was built, what it cost to make it fair, and every correction I had to publish along the way. If you want the number without the method, you already have it. HELUT is 15.1 percent slower than 16-worker Verilator on matched work. What follows is why I trust that figure more than the flattering one I started with.

scenes.label: SEALED RECEIPT PLAYBACK · final source and receipt hashes shown · no timing rerun
scenes.voiceover: Same circuit lineage on both sides. Same deterministic stimulus. Every digest matches, or the timings are void. Read the two scopes separately. BASELINE is the historical flattering row: HELUT's warmed synchronized graph call against a scalar native loop that also assigns, evaluates, reads, and hashes. It demonstrates sampled graph amortization, not end-to-end throughput. PAIRED is the accepted verdict: deterministic preparation, all input writes, synchronized execution, strict output readback, and the ordered digest counted on both sides, with Verilator using 16 persistent workers. At 65,536 lanes HELUT is 8.544 milliseconds and native is 7.422. HELUT remains 15.1 percent slower, and there is no paired crossover through the largest tested width. The next screen is correctness rather than speed: 65,536 different assignments and 589,824 output bits checked against their own oracles, with zero mismatches. Last, the teeth: corrupt lane 37 of 256 and the digest changes and the checker reports five mismatches. A gate that cannot fail is decoration.

scenes.headline: A two-state netlist, not a Verilog simulator
scenes.subhead: Yosys and ABC do the front end · B batches instances · N is wire degree
scenes.voiceover: First, what is actually in the comparison. HELUT is not a replacement for an event-driven simulator. Yosys does the front end and synthesis, ABC packs the gates into lookup tables, and HELUT starts from that two-state netlist of tables, flip-flops and ports. It has no model of behavioural Verilog, propagation delay, signal strength, or the X and Z values a real simulator tracks. So bit accuracy is not the selling point; Verilator and Icarus already own that. What the tensor form adds is two axes. B is how many independent copies of the circuit ride along together. N is how many coefficients stand in for one logical wire, where N equals one is plain Boolean and N equals 1,024 matches the polynomial size the encrypted side uses. Those axes expose parallel work. Whether the machine executes that work faster than a compiler does is the measurement, not the definition.

scenes.label: LIVE RUN · recorded 2026-09-05 · not a replay
scenes.voiceover: Same experiment, running now, not replayed. A synthesized Enigma rotor machine: 688 lookup tables, 26 flip-flops, 10 inputs, 8 outputs, evaluated as tensors at polynomial size 1024. Read the labels first, because the tool volunteers its own limits. Batch mode: legacy broadcast. Encoding: constant-fill, trivial, noise-free. That is not encrypted data and nothing pretends otherwise. Compile lands under 40 milliseconds. The first tick costs about 0.3 seconds because it pays to build and specialize the Metal kernels, and the 9 ticks after it average roughly 15 milliseconds. Then the gate that matters. A clear oracle written in Swift, which never touches the GPU, and the Metal path both produce the same 25 letters: KEINEBESONDERENEREIGNISSE. Result, PASS. Second screen, three more runs back to back: 66.5, 67.1, and 67.2 ticks per second. The run before them read 68.5. That spread across four passes in one sitting is why a single number here would be fiction.

scenes.kicker: The number that cannot be oversold
scenes.headline: The existing batch sweep repeats one feed
scenes.subhead: B=1000 is not yet 1000 independently checked vectors
scenes.voiceover: Now the caveat that used to undercut the most quotable number here, and the receipt that closed it. The old clock benchmark filled every batch lane with the same encoded value. Output tensors were written, but the timed loop never read them back and never hashed them per lane. That scaling table measured graph shape, allocation, and memory pressure, not useful work, and calling it a thousand-way verified simulation would have been a lie. Three things had to change before any batching claim was allowed: every lane doing independent work, a canonical checksum over ordered outputs, and a deliberately corrupted bit that makes the checksum fail. All three exist now. At B=65,536 the distinct-lane path carries 65,536 different input assignments, checks all 589,824 output bits against per-lane clear oracles, and reports 0 mismatches under one digest, with 511 distinct output signatures. And it has teeth: corrupting one lane moves the digest and surfaces the mismatch. That is verified batching, not proof of superior throughput.

scenes.kicker: The Reddit question, answered both ways
scenes.headline: Is it faster than native HDL?
scenes.subhead: Historical graph amortizes · paired scope remains 15.1% short
scenes.voiceover: For most of this project's life nobody had measured the native comparison. Now there is a Verilator baseline over the same emitted circuit lineage, the same deterministic assignments, and the same digest gate. The historical rows preserve the old scope: one warmed synchronized HELUT graph call versus a scalar Verilator loop that assigns, evaluates, reads, and hashes. Those rows can show a sampled HELUT win at large B, but the comparison is intentionally asymmetric and the sampled threshold moves between runs. The paired row is the result to hand a skeptic. It counts deterministic assignment and input packing, synchronized execution, strict readback and materialization, and the ordered digest on both sides, with native using 16 persistent workers. At B=65,536 HELUT measured 8.544 milliseconds versus native at 7.422. That is 1.151 times native, or 15.1 percent slower. No paired crossover was observed through B=65,536.

scenes.kicker: Profile first · preserve every failed claim
scenes.headline: We recovered the host path; native still leads
scenes.subhead: 32.414 ms → 8.544 ms HELUT · 1.122 ms paired gap remains
scenes.voiceover: The useful result is not just the final ratio; it is the recovery path. The original decomposed HELUT paired median at 65,536 lanes was 32.414 milliseconds. Flat lane-major output storage removed tens of thousands of tiny allocations. Precomputed port metadata and exact pointer decoding repaired assignment, packing, and readback overhead. A cost-selected constant-fill Shannon graph reduced the live logical arithmetic in this fixture from 1,116 operations to 194. Finally, an exact degree-one input pack kept every one of the 1,114,112 writes but cut the packing median from 1.240 milliseconds to 0.529. The final HELUT median is 8.544 milliseconds. Its phase medians are 0.030 for assignment, 0.529 for packing, 0.766 for graph execution, 0.548 for strict decode, and 6.677 for the ordered digest. Native is still ahead by 1.122 milliseconds. No one non-digest micro-phase is large enough to close that gap alone, so the next work is a combination, not a relabeled timer. One more thing the table says out loud: the paired ratio narrows at every width tested, from 77 times native at a single lane to 1.151 at 65,536, with no reversal. That is eight steps in one direction. It is also where the fixture ends, because 65,536 is the entire input space of a 16-bit adder, so a wider test needs a bigger circuit rather than a bigger batch.

scenes.headline: Shared work stays in the contract
scenes.subhead: Digest inside both timers · no post-hoc subtraction
scenes.voiceover: A previous draft tried to turn the shared digest into a separate evaluator headline. That was not defensible. Both backends hash the same lane, wire, and value words in the same order: 12 bytes per output bit, about 7.1 million bytes at 65,536 lanes. The accepted paired contract includes that work inside both timers. It is real output consumption and a correctness gate, not a tax we may remove after seeing the result. Native's narrower prepared timer excludes assignment and digest while including worker synchronization, evaluation, and output collection. HELUT's graph timer is a different boundary. Subtracting independent medians or comparing those unequal phases does not produce an honest native-evaluation ratio. The claim is therefore the direct paired result: 15.1 percent behind, digest included, no crossover through the tested range.

scenes.kicker: The contract was written first · one row is filled
scenes.headline: Same circuit. Same work. Same digest.
scenes.subhead: One combinational result · sequential and broader baselines still open
scenes.voiceover: The accepted comparison was frozen before its one retained run. One emitted Verilog circuit feeds both lineages. The lane corpus is deterministic and exhaustive at 65,536. HELUT rewrites every input buffer, executes one synchronized graph, strictly reads and materializes every output, and computes the canonical ordered digest. Native prepares every assignment, evaluates and stores every output with a persistent 16-worker pool, and computes the same digest. All of that stays inside the paired boundary. Five timed passes are retained at each of eight widths, and every raw array remains visible. This fills one bounded row: one combinational 8-bit ripple adder on one Mac. Still open are a sequential design with independent state per lane, an authored-RTL baseline beside the artifact-matched one, CXXRTL, other hosts, and a constant-total-work sweep. Naming the open rows is part of the result.

scenes.kicker: Why Enigma makes the architecture visible
scenes.headline: Build candidates on the CPU; sweep them on the GPU
scenes.subhead: Settings · tables · ciphertext · scores · survivors · repeat
scenes.voiceover: Enigma makes that pattern concrete. Host code organizes rotor, ring, and starting-position settings, plugboard pairs, and candidate populations. Wide Metal kernels sweep many settings or scoring lanes at once. The host then filters survivors, tightens constraints, breeds the next generation, and starts another round. With shared buffers those phases can live in one memory pool instead of paying a staging tax at every boundary. Large candidate tensors can spend real unified memory. But capacity is not throughput, and the repository has a receipt that proves it. At N=1024 and B=1000, resident memory peaked near 6 gigabytes and the tick rate fell to 13.62 per second, against roughly 69 at B=1. So the defensible claim is that unified memory opens this design space. Beating a discrete GPU inside it is a separate measurement nobody here has taken.

scenes.headline: The current verdict
bullets: Proved: supported Yosys LUT/DFF graphs execute on Metal
Measured: historical warmed graph can amortize against scalar native
Measured: paired HELUT is 15.1% slower at B=65,536
Required: identical ordered digest remains inside both timers
Observed: no paired crossover through B=65,536
Separate: million-lane HELUT graph sweep uses projected high-width native
Not claimed: encrypted speed, sequential lanes, Apple exclusivity
scenes.voiceover: So what does HELUT actually solve today? It bridges supported Yosys lookup-table graphs into a Metal tensor substrate, and that substrate agrees with independent clear checks bit for bit on the bounded receipts. The batch axis is verified rather than broadcast: 65,536 assignments, 589,824 output bits, zero mismatches, and a digest that moves under deliberate corruption. On performance, the historical warmed graph can amortize against a scalar native loop, but that is not the paired verdict. Under the accepted end-to-end boundary HELUT is 15.1 percent slower than 16-worker Verilator at 65,536 lanes, with no paired crossover through that width. The shared digest stays inside both timers, and no 12-fold evaluator result is synthesized from unequal phase boundaries. A separate HELUT graph sweep reaches a million lanes, but its high-width native line is projected on another fixture. Cleartext paired superiority remains unproved. The tensor path remains valuable for shared encrypted machinery and searchable truth tables, where the next episodes put different claims under different gates.

scenes.headline: If not better simulation, then what?
scenes.subhead: Next: melt the truth tables, freeze them again, and inspect the proof.
scenes.voiceover: The tensor path gets more interesting when the circuit is not merely executed. A lookup table can be lifted out of zeros and ones into continuous values, searched against a target, and pushed back toward discrete hardware. That is melt and freeze, and it arrives with its own bill. Did the frozen circuit stay correct? Did the topology change? Did the resource count improve? Will Yosys take the emitted result back? And what happens when the search refuses to go binary? Episode 15 puts the passing two-bit control, the round-trip checker, its negative control, and the failed M4 run on the same screen. It also answers the last question a skeptic asked me: how this compares with logic simplification that already exists. The combined search-and-map flow has been measured against an identical ABC recipe, and it came back a tie on every run.
